e.meaning: the East African country, named for Mount Kenya
e.etymology: Taken from the East African country, itself named for Mount Kenya. It came into use among African American families around 1970 as a name expressing pride in African heritage.
namesakes: Kenya Moore (former Miss USA and Real Housewives of Atlanta star)
Kenya Barris (creator of the sitcom Black-ish)

e.etymology: A spelling of Kiana, which is the Hawaiian form of Diana and also a Persian girls' name. In the US it took off in the 1990s alongside Tiana and Brianna.
A respelling of Brinley, an English surname and place name usually explained as burnt clearing. The Brynn spelling brings in Welsh bryn, hill, which is how many parents read it.

e.meaning: Eva, life, joined with Luna, moon
e.etymology: A joining of Eva, from Hebrew for life, and Luna, Latin and Spanish for moon. It recalls Isabel Allende's 1987 novel Eva Luna and is known through Venezuelan singer Evaluna Montaner.
A phonetic spelling of Nathan as English speakers say it, favored by Spanish-speaking families. Nathan is Hebrew natan, he gave, the name of a prophet in the time of King David.

e.meaning: form of Rosalind, later read as pretty rose
e.etymology: A spelling of Rosalyn, which comes from Rosaline and Rosalind. Rosalind began as a Germanic name and was later read as Spanish rosa linda, pretty rose.
namesakes: Rosalynn Carter (first lady, wife of Jimmy Carter)

e.etymology: An English occupational surname from Middle English sclater, a man who roofed buildings with slate.

assoc.t: A.C. Slater, the jock on Saved by the Bell
Kelly Slater, eleven-time world surfing champion

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins the Hux- of Huxley with the -ton ending of Paxton and Jaxton.
A modern American compound of the word name River and the -lynn ending of Brooklynn and Oaklynn.
A spelling variant of Nicholas that keeps the ck of Nick. Nicholas is from Greek Nikolaos, built from nike, victory, and laos, people.
An Arabic name for a fragrant flowering plant, also read as zayn ab, a father's adornment. It was borne by a daughter, a granddaughter and two wives of the Prophet Muhammad.

An English place name and surname from Old English scir, shire or bright, and leah, clearing. Once a man's name, it turned female after Charlotte Brontë's 1849 novel Shirley and soared with Shirley Temple.
namesakes: Shirley Temple (child film star of the 1930s)
Shirley Chisholm (first Black woman elected to Congress)

assoc.t: Shirley Temple, the nonalcoholic drink named for the star

e.note: Invites the Airplane! joke: Surely you can't be serious. Don't call me Shirley.

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Eve, Chavah, from the root for to live. In Genesis she is named as the mother of all the living.
namesakes: Chava (Tevye's third daughter in Fiddler on the Roof)
e.note: In Mexican Spanish chava is slang for a girl and Chava is a nickname for Salvador; some will say CHAH-vuh.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Uzzi'el, my strength is God. Several men in the Old Testament bear it, among them Uzziel son of Kohath, a grandson of Levi. Today it is used by Hispanic and Jewish families.
e.note: The short form Uzi is also the name of an Israeli submachine gun.

e.meaning: from Percy, a village in Normandy
e.etymology: From the Percys, Norman lords of Northumberland, named for Percy-en-Auge in Normandy. Their surname became a first name, and Percy also serves as a short form of Percival.
namesakes: Percy Weasley (Ron's older brother in Harry Potter)

assoc.t: Percy Jackson, demigod hero of Rick Riordan's novels
Percy, the small green engine in Thomas & Friends
Percy or Perc, slang for a Percocet pill

e.etymology: A respelling of Weston, an English place name and surname from Old English west and tun, the western settlement. Westen also happens to be the German word for west.
The English word unique, borrowed from French and going back to Latin unicus, only or sole. As a US given name it was most used in the 1990s and early 2000s.
e.note: Sometimes used as a punchline in jokes about unusual names.

e.etymology: A spelling of Kaylee, a late-20th-century name built from Kay and the -lee ending that spread in many spellings.

assoc.t: 2008 death of toddler Caylee Anthony and the trial after

e.meaning: morning star; one who knocks at night
e.etymology: From Arabic tariq, one who knocks at the door by night, and so the morning star, the title of sura 86 of the Quran. Tariq ibn Ziyad led the conquest of Spain in 711, and Gibraltar is named for him.
namesakes: Tariq St. Patrick (lead character of Power Book II: Ghost)

e.meaning: lily; in modern Hebrew also rose
e.etymology: Hebrew shoshanah, lily, a word traced to the Egyptian for lotus; in modern Hebrew it also means rose. Through Greek Sousanna it is the source of Susanna and Susan.
A modern American coinage, a C spelling of Kamari, which is modeled on Amari and Jamari.
The Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Oswald, through Late Latin Osvaldus, from Germanic words for a god and for rule or power. Saint Oswald was a 7th-century king of Northumbria.
A short form of Alessandra, the Italian form of Alexandra, from Greek alexein, to defend, and aner, man. Its sound sits between Alexa and Alyssa.

assoc.t: Alessa Gillespie, the girl at the heart of Silent Hill

e.etymology: A modern American coinage in the family of Jamarion and Damarion, built on Marion or Amari with a Ka- opening.

e.meaning: from the Roman family name Terentius
e.etymology: A spelling of Terence, from Terentius, a Roman family name of obscure origin borne by the playwright Terence and by early saints. In Ireland it was used to render the Gaelic name Turlough.
namesakes: Terrence Howard (actor in Hustle & Flow and Empire)

e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English ham, home, or hean, high, and tun, settlement. It has been used as a first name in the US since the 19th century.

assoc.t: The Hamptons, wealthy Long Island beach resorts
Hampton Inn, Hilton's mid-priced hotel chain
Hampton, Virginia, home of Hampton University
Fred Hampton, Black Panther leader killed in 1969

e.etymology: The Hebrew word for comfort or consolation, from the same root as the men's names Nachum and Menachem. It is a traditional name in Orthodox Jewish communities.
A modern name that grew out of Sheila and Shea, with the -ayla sound of Kayla and Layla. Sheila is the English spelling of Irish Síle, a form of Cecilia.
e.note: My Shayla is a 2024 TikTok catchphrase for someone dearly loved, from a tearful Tyrese Gibson video about his daughter.

e.etymology: The feminine of Wilhelm, the German form of William, from Germanic wil, will or desire, and helm, helmet or protection. It dates from the 17th century and was borne by a queen of the Netherlands.
namesakes: Queen Wilhelmina (queen of the Netherlands from 1890 to 1948)
Wilhelmina Slater (Vanessa Williams's character on Ugly Betty)

e.etymology: The feminine of Latin Callistus, from Greek kallistos, most beautiful, the superlative of kalos. Compare the nymph Callisto. Actress Calista Flockhart made it familiar in the late 1990s.
A spelling of Levi better known as a Jewish surname. Levi, Jacob's third son and ancestor of the Levites, has a name that Genesis explains as joined or attached.

assoc.t: levy, the English word for a tax or a seizure for debt
Eugene and Dan Levy, father and son of Schitt's Creek

e.note: Spelled like the word levy, a tax, said LEV-ee; expect to explain whether yours is said like Levi.

e.etymology: The Turkish and Persian form of Arabic diya, light or radiance. It is a man's name in Turkey; in the US it is given mostly to girls, alongside Zia and Zoya.
